items.title: Benny Waters interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995
items.q: And on tenor, there was no one in that period but Coleman Hawkins. Because he was the greatest of all at that period, see?

ctx.x: You know you are known as a person who continually updates your skills and your sounds, always listening to new artists and picking up new ideas. And can you tell us about that? Just the process of hearing new things and bringing them into your repertoire of sounds.

Well this can be explained, I’ll tell you why, because I don’t never get tired of listening, you know? And I listen to everybody, everything. I listen to free jazz. I listen to bebop. I listen to fusion. And I find I get something from everything. Dixieland. I worked in a Dixieland band three years at Jimmy Ryan’s. So, I worked in a blues band, see for a year and a half. So I didn’t like the band so well, see but the guy liked me so I stayed there see until I got tired and I left. But if it seems that I play…

Not exclusive, but I made several arrangements for him, see? And then the next was Benny Carter, the young Benny Carter. That’s on alto. And on tenor, there was no one in that period but Coleman Hawkins. Because he was the greatest of all at that period, see? Then you listen to everybody else, see, so you can get something from everybody.

items.title: 68002_Benny Waters oral history interview
items.q: my inspiration was Coleman Hawkins, it was that slap tongue... And that was taken strictly from Coleman Hawkins. See, so I was copying then.

ctx.x: Well, I could improvise, I always could improvise. I mean I knew harmony from, just from natural ability, I always could improvise. See, that's why I didn't like to - I was glad to be with this band because I had a chance to, more so than with my brother, all those dance bands. Dance band is commercial gig, you just play the music where it is and you get paid, but I mean, even big bands you don't - even big bands, that's, I'm sure of this, but I'm pretty sure a lot of these fine saxophonists, jazz men who left…

number had something there for tenor, see. But otherwise you don't get a chance to play. That's why Procope went back musically, I mean as far as choruses are concerned, on his horns. Procope was a great saxophone player then, on the period he was working with Kirby, you understand? But when he worked with these big bands playing first, he didn't get the chance, there was too many others. When this is, like Johnny Hodg[es] and those guys, they would favor them, see, so he didn't have a chance to play as much. So…
